title: New $La_{2/3-x}Sr_xLi_xTiO_3$ Solid Solution: Structure, Microstructure, and Li<sup>+</sup> Conductivity

structure.title: Abstract / Introduction
structure.text:
Ainhoa Morata-Orrantia, Susana García-Martín,\* and Miguel Ángel Alario-Franco

Departamento de Química Inorgánica, Facultad de Ciencias Químicas, Universidad Complutense, 28040 Madrid, Spain

Received June 1, 2002. Revised Manuscript Received September 30, 2002

The stoichiometry range, crystal chemistry, ionic conductivity, and electrochemical window of the  $La_{2/3-x}Sr_xLi_xTiO_3$  system with a perovskite-related structure have been studied. The range of existence of the solid solution is  $(0.06 \le x \le 0.3)$ . Powder X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy results show that these oxides have a unit cell multiple of the perovskite cell with dimensions  $a \approx \sqrt{2} a_p$ ,  $b \approx \sqrt{2} a_p$ , and  $c \approx 2a_p$ . The ionic conductivity of the material and its dependence on composition and temperature have been examined by complex impedance spectroscopy. Lithium ion conductivity increases with increasing lithium content up to the value 7.12  $10^{-5}$  S·cm<sup>-1</sup> at room temperature, corresponding to x = 0.25. Electrochemical experiments indicate that these materials can be used as solid electrolytes in secondary batteries having Li metal as the anode down to 1.75 V.

structure.title: Introduction
structure.text:
Lithium batteries are among the most promising power sources for the future due to their high energy density and good cycling life. In particular, all-solidstate lithium batteries allow fabrication of compact and leak proof batteries of different shapes and sizes. Therefore, research on materials as potential electrolytes in solid-state lithium batteries is an interesting area of solid-state science.

The compounds of general formula La<sub>2/3-x</sub>Li<sub>3x</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub> have the highest lithium conductivity at room temperature ( $\sigma_{\rm bulk} \approx 1 \times 10^{-3} \, \rm S \cdot cm^{-1}$ ) reported to date. <sup>1-5</sup> Pure phases are found for a range of compositions corresponding to  $0.036 \le x \le 0.14,^{3.6}$  and the oxides have a crystal structure related to the perovskite type (ABO<sub>3</sub>) with A-cation deficiency. Other systems such as  $RE_{2/3-x^{-1}}$  $Li_{3x}TiO_3$  (RE = Pr, Nd, Sm) have been studied,<sup>3,6–8</sup> but in all of them it has so far been found that the lithium conductivity is lower than that in the La system. No significant changes are seen in the crystal structure apart from the change in size of the unit cell. It then seems that the decrease of the RE-O distances (as a consequence of the smaller ionic radii of Pr, Nd, and Sm compared to La) reduces the bottleneck size, dis-

turbing the Li<sup>+</sup> ion migration via A-size vacancies. Moreover, in situ experiments concerning the ionic conductivity dependence on mechanical pressure for La<sub>0.52</sub>Li<sub>0.35</sub>TiO<sub>2.96</sub> indicate that the conductivity decreases when the pressure increases, 9 i.e., the pressure effect on the ionic conductivity seems to be equivalent to the A-size substitution effect. Therefore, increasing the A–O distances could eventually improve the lithium conductivity of these materials.

The perovskite structure tolerates total or partial substitution of the A and B cations by ions with different valence states. Sr<sup>2+</sup> and Ba<sup>2+</sup> are bigger cations than La<sup>3+</sup>, so it is interesting to study the influence on the ionic conductivity of the substitution of La<sup>3+</sup> in the  $La_{2/3-x}Li_{3x}TiO_3$  system by these divalent cations. In this sense, an increase of the bulk ionic conductivity ( $\sigma_{\text{bulk}}$ )  $\approx 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \; \text{S} \cdot \text{cm}^{-1}$ ) has been reported in the (La<sub>1/2</sub>- $\text{Li}_{1/2}$ )<sub>1-x</sub> $M_x$ TiO<sub>3</sub> (M = Sr, Ba) oxides for M = Sr and x = 0.05.4 More recently, a slight improvement of the lithium conductivity ( $\sigma_{300\text{K}} \approx 1.12 \times 10^{-3} \text{ S} \cdot \text{cm}^{-1}$ ) has been demonstrated in  $La_{0.57-2x/3}Sr_xLi_{0.3}TiO_3$  for x =0.08.<sup>10</sup> In this paper, we report the simultaneous lanthanum substitution by strontium and lithium addition in the system La<sub>2/3-x</sub>Sr<sub>x</sub>Li<sub>x</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub>. This system allows us to study the ionic conductivity dependence on both the size of the crystal unit cell and the carrier concentration. We present here our data concerning the stoichiometry range, crystal chemistry, and lithium ion conductivity, as well as the electrochemical window versus Li, for the La<sub>2/3-x</sub>Sr<sub>x</sub>Li<sub>x</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub> solid solution.

The molar ratio of the metals in the compounds was determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectroscopy (ICP-MS) and X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (XRFS). For ICP-MS we used a Perkin-Elmer Elan 6000 with autosampler AS. To perform the ICP analysis, a solution protocol was optimized. Samples were treated with a mixture of nitric, hydrochloric, and hydrofluric acids in a 3:2:1 molar ratio at 150 °C in a CEM microwave furnace digestor (MDS-2000 model) with temperature and pressure sensors. Because of La<sup>3+</sup> precipitation during the dilution with the acid solution, XRFS was used to analyze this cation using a Bruker S4 Explorer.

Crystalline phase identification and determination of the lattice parameters were carried out by powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) using a Philips X'PERT diffractometer with Cu Kα1 radiation, a curved Cu monochromator, and the Philips X'PERT PEAPD software. The patterns were taken at step mode with a step size equal to 0.02 ( $2\theta$  degrees) and time per step equal to 10 s.

Compositions out of this range were multiphase. Comparing this composition range with that corresponding to other systems, such as RE2/3-xLi3xTiO3 (RE = La, Nd, Pr)3,6,8 and La2/3LixTi1-xAlxO3, 12 led to the conclusion that this kind of solid solution seems to admit a number of vacancies within the A positions up to about 27% and down to about 4%, under the preparation conditions described. Table 1 shows the chemical composition analysis results of three samples with different x values. Owing to the good agreement between analytical and nominal values, nominal compositions will be used in the following. Figure 1a shows the powder X-ray diffraction patterns of four samples quenched from the temperature of synthesis. The oxides with x = 0.3, 0.2 have a perovskite-type structure. Superlattice reflections with respect to the ideal cubic perovskite structure are observed in the patterns corresponding to x = 0.06, 0.1. These reflections are broad and have low intensity in the patterns for x = 0.1 but are well defined when the sample is annealed at a temperature lower than that during the synthesis. Figure 1b shows the powder XRD patterns of four oxides annealed at 1000 °C and quenched from this temperature. We can see that the intensity of the superlattice reflections increases when annealing the oxides with $0.06 \le x \le 0.15$ . However, no extra reflections appear at any annealing temperature in the patterns of the oxides with $0.15 \le x \le 0.3$ . The superlattice reflections double the $c_p$ lattice parameter (p refers to the cubic perovskite unit cell). According to all these intensity maxima, the unit cell of the materials is either $2a_p \times 2a_p \times 2a_p$ or $\sqrt{2}$ $a_p \times$ $\sqrt{2}$ $a_p \times 2a_p$ ; but, in this second case, the crystals should be twinned due to the different orientations of the *c*-axis. Electron microscopy was used to clarify which of the two possibilities correspond to our materials. Figure 3 shows the HRTEM image of the [001]p zone axis of the sample with x = 0.06 quenched from the synthesis temperature. The crystal has three different domains: one domain with image difference contrasts corresponding to 2ap periodicity along the [001]p direction; another domain showing the $2a_p$ periodicity along $[010]_p$ direction; and the third domain with $\sqrt{2}a_p$ periodicity along the [110]p direction. The image confirms that the unit cell of the material is $\sqrt{2}$ $a_p \times \sqrt{2}$ $a_p \times 2a_p$ and that the crystal is formed by three sets of domains with different orientation of the *c*-axis within each of them. Coming back to the SAED patterns, it is important to comment that far away from the origin, splitting of some reflections into two can be seen (see arrows in the patterns of the [110]p and [001]p zone axes of Figure 2). All the samples have similar SAED patterns with no obvious dependence on either annealing temperature or composition, indicating that the crystal structure of all these materials is based in the unit cell $\sqrt{2}$ $a_p \times \sqrt{2}$ $a_p$ $\times$ 2ap. nodes.title: Perovskite Distortion, Cation Ordering, and Lattice Parameters
nodes.text: The 2a<sub>p</sub> periodicity is observed in small regions of the crystal of just two or three times the size of the unit cell dimensions. These crystals are not formed by large domains but by very small ones showing the three different orientations of the *c*-axis. The most common distortion of the perovskite structure consists of the tilting of the BO<sub>6</sub> octahedra, leading to the  $\sqrt{2}$   $a_p \times \sqrt{2}$   $a_p \times 2a_p$  unit cell. Tilting of the  $TiO_6$ octahedra must occur in our materials to accommodate the size of the A cations (La<sup>3+</sup>, Li<sup>+</sup>, and Sr<sup>2+</sup>), to attain the appropriate A-O distances. Moreover, an ordering of the A cations could also exist. It has, in fact, been reported in other compounds with perovskite-related structure that the presence of the (0 0 1/2) reflection in the powder X-ray diffraction patterns indicates an A-cation ordering perpendicular to the c-axis. However, the intensity of this reflection seems to depend on the size of the diffracting crystal domains. Our results show that the samples giving X-ray diffraction patterns with strong  $(0 \ 0 \ 1/2)_p$  reflection are characterized by relatively big domains in the crystals (Figure 3) whereas very broad reflections are observed in the case of a microdomain texture (Figure 4). The powder X-ray diffraction patterns of the oxides have, consequently, been indexed using the orthorhombic unit cell  $\sqrt{2}$   $a_p \times \sqrt{2}$   $a_p \times 2a_p$  so as to calculate the variation of the cell size with La<sup>3+</sup> substitution. Table 2 shows the lattice parameters of some oxides with different composition. The lattice parameters increase when x increases, as it is expected of the substitution of La<sup>3+</sup> by Sr<sup>2+</sup> and Li<sup>+</sup> (Sr<sup>2+</sup> has a larger ionic radius than La3+ at equal coordination).

The data fit an Arrhenius-type equation  $\sigma = \sigma_0 e^{-Ea/kT}$  where  $E_a$  is the activation energy of the process. nodes.title: Electrochemical Performance and Li+ Intercalation
nodes.text:
Figure 8a shows a cyclic voltammogram, and Figure 8b shows the voltagecomposition curves for three charge and discharge cycles of a cell using the oxide with x = 0.25 as working electrode. Strong cathodic peaks are observed in the voltammogram: the peak at 1.5 V is associated with the reduction of Ti<sup>4+</sup> to Ti<sup>3+</sup> due to the electrochemical Li<sup>+</sup> intercalation into the material, and the peak at 0.7 V is ascribed to the decomposition of the electrolyte. In accordance with the potentiostatic experiment is the galvanostatic one, which shows that the material can reversibly insert up to 0.17 mol of lithium atoms per formula unit from 1.75 to 1 V. The very small losses in capacity in the charge processes are most probably associated with the loss of electrical contact between some cathode particles. As a result of the intercalation reaction and therefore, the reduction of Ti<sup>4+</sup>, electronic conductivity appears in the oxide. This means that the oxide can be used as a solid electrolyte in secondary batteries having Li metal as anode down to 1.75 V.

**Acknowledgment.
